summary: This standards-track document defines an IPv6 header compression format for 6LoWPANs, updating RFC 4944. It uses shared context to compress arbitrary prefixes. It shrinks packets for tiny low-power radio networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6282 defines ways to shorten IPv6 headers on small IEEE 802.15.4 networks. Devices can omit information they can reconstruct from shared context, link-layer addresses, or standard values.

questions: how to compress ipv6 for sensor networks
how small can an ipv6 header get on 802.15.4
subtitle: How IPv6 and following headers are compressed for IEEE 802.15.4 networks.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 frames have limited payload space, and the earlier RFC 4944 compression format was insufficient for many routable IPv6 packets.
tldr.mechanism: LOWPAN_IPHC encodes common IPv6 values and address information compactly, using link-layer addresses or shared context. LOWPAN_NHC can compress following headers, including UDP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6282 updates RFC 4944. It makes the older compression format NOT RECOMMENDED for new senders while requiring updated implementations to process the new format; RFC 8066 later updates RFC 6282.

facts.label: UDP ports compressible to four bits

today: RFC 6282 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944 and is updated by RFC 8066. RFC 6282 says sending packets with the older RFC 4944 compression is NOT RECOMMENDED for new implementations.

sections.title: Why a New Compression Format Was Needed
sections.content:
IEEE 802.15.4 has an MTU of 127 bytes and about 80 octets of MAC payload with security enabled. RFC 4944 introduced LOWPAN_HC1 and LOWPAN_HC2 to carry IPv6 over these constrained links.

The older format worked best for link-local traffic, where addresses could be reconstructed from link-layer addresses. Routable addresses often needed their prefixes and interface identifiers carried in the packet, and multicast addresses could require all 128 bits. RFC 6282 defines LOWPAN_IPHC for IPv6 addresses and LOWPAN_NHC for compressing following headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Small radio frames leave little room for an IPv6 header. The earlier format could shorten some local addresses, but often could not shorten addresses used beyond the local link.

sections.title: How the New Format Relates to RFC 4944
sections.content:
LOWPAN_IPHC is intended to replace the compression in Section 10 of RFC 4944. Implementing that old section is NOT RECOMMENDED. New implementations MAY decompress packets using it, but SHOULD NOT send packets in that format. Updated implementations MUST process packets that use RFC 6282.

The RFC 4944 fragmentation rules remain in effect. Fragment sizes and offsets refer to the IPv6 datagram before compression, so a header that cannot fit in the first fragment MUST NOT be compressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The new format replaces the old header-shortening rules. Devices must be able to read the new format, while new senders should stop using the old one.

sections.title: The LOWPAN_IPHC Header
sections.content:
LOWPAN_IPHC uses a two-octet base encoding, with an optional context-identifier octet. The base fields describe how Traffic Class, Flow Label, Next Header, Hop Limit, and source and destination addresses are represented. Fields that remain in the packet follow the encoding.

The format assumes common cases such as IPv6 version 6, zero Traffic Class and Flow Label, a Payload Length inferred from lower layers, familiar Hop Limit values, and addresses derived from link-layer addresses or a small set of prefixes. The Version field is always omitted and Payload Length MUST always be omitted.

In the best case, link-local communication needs two octets for dispatch and IPHC encoding. The RFC gives a seven-octet IPv6 header representation for routing over multiple IP hops; the Hop Limit remains in-line because forwarding changes it at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: A short field tells the receiver which parts of the IPv6 header were left out. The receiver uses that information and the agreed rules to rebuild the header.

sections.title: Rebuilding Addresses from Context
sections.content:
Address-mode bits say whether the packet carries a full address, only some address bits, or none. In stateless mode, the receiver can restore link-local prefix bits. In stateful mode, it uses a context, which is information shared by the compressor and decompressor, to restore prefixes.

The format supports up to 16 contexts. When the Context Identifier Extension is present, its two four-bit fields identify the source and destination contexts; context zero is the default. How nodes share, maintain, or recover context is outside this RFC's scope.

An omitted interface identifier can be derived from the encapsulating header. An extended IEEE 802.15.4 address is mapped as in RFC 4291 by inverting the universal/local bit. A 16-bit short address maps to an identifier of the form 0000:00ff:fe00:XXXX; bits may be omitted only when they match the defined mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: If both devices know a prefix, the packet can carry fewer address bits. The receiver combines those bits with the matching shared context to rebuild the address.

sections.title: Traffic Values and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
The TF field controls which parts of Traffic Class and Flow Label are carried in-line. Some combinations let the encoder omit one or both values. The Traffic Class is rearranged in the compressed form so the ECN bits appear in a consistent position.

Stateless multicast compression can carry 48, 32, or 8 bits instead of a full 128-bit address for supported address forms. Stateful compression can use a context for unicast-prefix-based multicast addresses and carry six octets. Other stateful multicast mode values are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic labels have common values, the encoding can leave them out. Some multicast addresses also have shorter forms that preserve the information needed to rebuild them.

sections.title: Compressing Following Headers and UDP
sections.content:
When the IPHC Next Header bit indicates compression, the following bytes begin a LOWPAN_NHC encoding. Encoded headers must be contiguous, with each one preceded by an IPHC or NHC encoding. This RFC defines encodings for IPv6 extension headers and UDP.

The UDP encoding can shorten ports in the range 0xf0b0 to 0xf0bf to four bits. Other port patterns use more bits. The UDP Length field MUST always be omitted and inferred from lower layers.

A compressor MAY omit the UDP checksum only when the upper layer authorizes it and the required integrity protections are in place. The compressor must verify the checksum before omitting it; the decompressor must restore it, verify the additional integrity check, and drop the packet if it cannot confirm that check.
sections.plainLanguage: The format can shorten headers that follow IPv6, including UDP. It can omit a UDP checksum only when another authorized integrity check protects the same information.

fields.name: TF
fields.desc: Traffic Class and Flow Label handling.

fields.name: NH
fields.desc: 1 means the next header uses LOWPAN_NHC.

fields.name: HLIM
fields.desc: Hop Limit in-line or represented as 1, 64, or 255.

fields.name: CID
fields.desc: 1 means a Context Identifier Extension follows.
